## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over 35 years. The North China Plain is wheat-maize country — that's what the soil, the markets, and the infrastructure here are built around. I'm not going to change that.

My land is about 10 mu. I'll do winter wheat on all of it, then turn it over to summer maize right after wheat harvest in June. That's the rotation I've run my whole life and it works.

For wheat, I'll use Kenong 199 — it's a proven improved variety that handles our dry conditions well and the county agricultural station has been recommending it for years. I read enough to know the newer drought-tolerant lines are worth the extra seed cost. I'll apply base fertilizer before sowing and topdress at jointing. Three irrigations: one before winter freeze, one at jointing, one at heading. That's already cutting back from what my father used to do — the water table has dropped badly here and I feel the responsibility to not over-pump.

For maize, I'll go with Xianyu 335 — reliable hybrid, good standability, and it machines well at harvest which matters now that I'm 60 and hire out the combine. I'll direct-seed into the wheat stubble with no-tillage to save time and moisture. Summer rains usually cover most of the water needs; I'll only irrigate once if we hit a dry spell in August.

I'll apply herbicide after each planting, and I'll spray fungicide on the wheat at heading — rust and powdery mildew are real risks here. For maize I'll watch for fall armyworm, which has been spreading north. One pesticide pass should be enough if I catch it early.

I use rotary tillage before wheat to break up the compaction, but I skip tillage for the maize — saves diesel and protects the soil structure.
